questions.q: What are the two categories of quantum test the lesson identifies?
options: Unit tests and integration tests
Construction tests (deterministic, pre-execution) and statistical tests (post-execution, measurement outcomes)
Fast tests and slow tests
Simulator tests and hardware tests
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction is construction tests, which check circuit structure deterministically before execution, versus statistical tests, which check measurement outcomes after execution and require a tolerance rather than exact equality.

questions.q: Why is testing that an oracle circuit has X gates on exactly the correct qubits a construction test rather than a statistical one?
options: Because it checks the circuit's structure before any execution, which is deterministic and should produce the identical pass/fail result on every run
Because oracle circuits never contain X gates
Because it still requires running the circuit many times
Because construction tests are a synonym for statistical tests
questions.explain: Checking gate placement and qubit wiring examines the circuit object itself, never executing it -- so the result is deterministic and reproducible, the defining property of a construction test.

questions.q: Why can't you write `assert counts == {'0': 512, '1': 512}` to test that a Hadamard gate produces a fair coin flip?
options: Because Hadamard gates don't produce measurable outcomes
Because measurement is a random sample, so even correct code will almost never produce an exact 512/512 split
Because Python dictionaries cannot be compared with ==
Because 512/512 is mathematically impossible for a fair coin
questions.explain: Measurement outcomes are random samples from the expected distribution. Even on perfectly correct code, an exact 512/512 split is unlikely on any given run -- the test needs a calculated tolerance instead, built in Lesson 7.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does it mean when a statistical test fails intermittently on code that hasn't changed?
options: It means you should re-run the test until it passes and move on
It usually indicates the tolerance is too tight for the shot count being used -- a test design issue to fix deliberately, not a fluke to dismiss
It means the quantum backend is permanently broken
It means construction tests are no longer needed
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues that re-running until it passes is backwards; intermittent failure on unchanged correct code points to a tolerance/shot-count mismatch that should be fixed deliberately, with the fix detailed in Lesson 7.

questions.q: Why does a statistical test need a stated confidence level (e.g. alpha=0.01) while a construction test does not?
options: Construction tests are less important so they don't need any rigor

A statistical test has a built-in, calculable error rate due to sampling randomness that must be explicitly acknowledged, while a deterministic construction test either passes or fails identically every time
Confidence levels are a Qiskit-specific requirement with no general meaning
Construction tests already include a confidence level by default
questions.explain: Because a statistical test's outcome is itself a sample, it carries an inherent, calculable chance of a false negative or false positive -- stating a confidence level makes that error rate explicit. A deterministic construction test has no such randomness to account for.
